content.title: About
content.content: Bread, marble rye and pumpernickel are three types of whole‑grain breads made from a blend of wheat, rye and whole‑grain flours. Marble rye features a distinctive swirled pattern of light and dark dough, while pumpernickel is a dense, dark loaf enriched with molasses or honey for a deep, slightly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Marble rye gets its name from the marble‑like swirl created when light and dark batters are folded together.
Pumpernickel originated in Germany and is traditionally considered a “sturdy” bread because of its high fiber and mineral content.
Combining different flours increases the bioavailability of B‑vitamins and minerals such as iron and magnesium.
Whole‑grain breads stay fresh longer than white breads due to lower sugar content.
In some cultures marble rye is served with soups, while pumpernickel is popular for open‑face sandwiches with smoked fish.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain breads provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health and promoting satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain flour supplies thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and folate, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The breads contain iron, magnesium, zinc and selenium, which contribute to hemoglobin formation and immune support.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white bread, whole‑grain varieties cause a slower rise in blood glucose, beneficial for weight management and diabetes control.

items.title: Supports gut microbiome
items.content: Prebiotic fibers in whole grains feed beneficial bacteria, helping maintain a healthy intestinal flora.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat and rye breads contain gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some loaves may contain significant salt; individuals with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although healthier than white bread, these breads are still calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Phytic acid in whole grains can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or fermenting the dough lowers its level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the breads as a snack, for sandwiches, toast, or alongside soups and salads. Marble rye pairs well with soft cheese, while pumpernickel is excellent with smoked fish, pâté or mustard.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the breads in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature to keep the crust crisp. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag and thaw as needed.

chicken-breast-sauteed-skin-not-eaten.title: Chicken Breast, Sauteed, Skin Not Eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken breast that has been quickly sauteed in a small amount of oil. The cooking method retains most nutrients while keeping the fat content low.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast provides more protein per 100 g than most other meat cuts.
High‑heat, short‑time sauteing helps lock in moisture and flavor.
Without skin, the calorie count is far lower than that of thighs or drumsticks.
Chicken is a good source of vitamin B6, which supports amino‑acid metabolism.
Around the world the breast is prepared in many ways, from simple sauté to complex sauces and marinades.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving delivers about 31 g of complete protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skinless breast contains roughly 3 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in vitamin B6 and niacin, which aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium and modest amounts of iron, important for bone health and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: High leucine content promotes muscle‑protein synthesis, beneficial for active individuals.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may contain Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small proportion of people are allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: If the breast is marinated, watch added salt to stay within daily sodium limits.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Very high‑temperature cooking can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; avoid over‑cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the breast into strips, quickly sauté in olive or vegetable oil, and season with herbs, spices, or lemon juice. Serve in salads, sandwiches, with vegetable sides, or use in stir‑fries and wraps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh breast refrigerated at +2‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen breast lasts up to 9 months at –18 °C. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken Kiev is a classic Russian dish consisting of a chicken breast fillet that is butter‑filled with herbs, breaded, and fried until golden. When cooked correctly, the butter melts inside, creating a juicy, aromatic center.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the early 20th century and quickly became a staple in Soviet restaurants.
The traditional recipe uses butter mixed with parsley and dill for the filling.
There are many variations of the stuffing, including cheese, mushrooms, nuts, or dried fruit.
Chicken Kiev is often served with mashed potatoes or a vegetable side.
In many Western countries the dish is known as “Chicken Kiev,” though the original Russian version differs from some adaptations.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken meat provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: The fillet contains vitamins B3, B6, and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: The butter filling supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids important for heart health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish offers phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, which contribute to bone strength and immune support.

items.title: Herb antioxidants
items.content: Parsley and dill add vitamins C and A as well as antioxidant compounds.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because of the butter and breading, the dish is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Butter may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Risk of hot butter splatter
items.content: Improper cooking can cause the butter to burst out of the fillet, leading to burns.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Salt used in the breading can be a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Chicken Kiev hot, cutting into it with a knife to reveal the melted butter. It pairs well with mashed potatoes, boiled rice, fresh vegetables, or a light salad. Let the dish rest for 2‑3 minutes after plating so the juices redistribute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked Chicken Kiev in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Frozen portions can be stored for up to 3 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating in the oven to retain a crisp crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Coconut milk is a thick, creamy, white liquid made by blending grated coconut flesh with water and straining it. It has a rich, sweet, nutty coconut flavor and is used in curries, soups, desserts, smoothies, and as a dairy-free milk alternative. Canned coconut milk is thick and rich, while carton coconut milk drinks are thinner and diluted.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coconut milk is not the same as coconut water, which is the thin liquid found inside young coconuts.
Canned coconut milk separates into a thick cream layer on top and a thinner liquid below.
Coconut milk is a staple in Southeast Asian, South Asian, Caribbean, and Pacific Island cooking.
It is naturally dairy-free and lactose-free.
Coconut cream is a thicker, richer version with less water.

items.title: Dairy-free and lactose-free
items.content: Coconut milk is suitable for people who avoid dairy.

items.title: Provides manganese and copper
items.content: Coconut milk contains manganese and copper, which support metabolism.

items.title: Contains medium-chain fats
items.content: Coconut milk contains medium-chain triglycerides, a type of fat that is digested differently from other fats.

items.title: Provides iron and magnesium
items.content: Coconut milk provides small amounts of iron and magnesium.

items.title: Adds richness and flavor
items.content: A little coconut milk adds creaminess to dishes without dairy.

items.title: High in saturated fat and calories
items.content: Canned coconut milk is very high in saturated fat and calories, so portions should be small.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Coconut allergy is uncommon but can occur.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts may cause bloating or loose stools in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Additives and added sugar
items.content: Some products contain thickeners such as guar gum, preservatives, or added sugar, so check labels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coconut milk can be stirred into curries, soups, stews, rice, porridge, sauces, desserts, smoothies, and coffee. Shake the can well before opening, or use the thick cream layer for richer dishes. Use light coconut milk for a thinner, lower-fat version.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened canned coconut milk in a cool, dry place. Once opened, transfer it to an airtight container, refrigerate it, and use it within four to five days, or freeze it for longer storage. Shake or stir before using, since it separates.

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are the young pods of the common bean harvested before the seeds fully mature. When cooked they retain a bright green color, a tender flavor and a slight crunch. They are widely used as a side dish, in salads, soups and stews.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans belong to the legume family and are among the oldest cultivated crops.
In the United States they are often called “string beans” because of the thin fiber running along the pod, which is usually removed before cooking.
Cooked green beans contain more vitamin C than many other vegetables, though some is lost with prolonged boiling.
In Japan the beans are commonly served as “edamame” – boiled in salted water and eaten whole.
There are over 100 varieties of green beans, differing in size, shape and flavor.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports normal bowel function, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood glucose levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked beans provides about 2 g of protein, making them a useful addition to vegetarian and vegan diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Green beans contain folate (B9), thiamine (B1) and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They provide iron, magnesium, potassium and copper, supporting blood formation, muscle function and energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Green beans are virtually fat‑free, making them suitable for low‑calorie eating plans.

items.title: Raw beans may contain toxins
items.content: Uncooked beans can contain phytohaemagglutinin, a compound that can cause food poisoning. Proper cooking destroys the toxin.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to legumes, experiencing skin or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Vitamin C loss with overcooking
items.content: To preserve vitamin C, beans should be boiled no longer than 5‑7 minutes and then shocked in ice water.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Typically beans are boiled in salted water for 5‑7 minutes until tender, then quickly cooled to keep their vivid color. They can be tossed into salads, pastas, soups, stews, or served as a simple side with olive oil and lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Freshly harvested beans keep in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 5 days. Frozen beans retain quality for up to 8 months; thaw before use and briefly re‑heat if needed.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef stew with pasta is a hearty dish where tender pieces of beef are slowly cooked in a flavorful broth together with pasta. The meal is rich in protein, iron, and carbohydrates, making it an excellent option for replenishing energy after physical activity.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional beef stew is cooked in a covered pot, which helps retain maximum flavor and nutrients.
Short‑shaped pasta (penne, rigatoni) is usually chosen because it holds the sauce well.
Beef provides a higher level of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.
Low‑heat braising makes the meat extra tender and develops deep flavor notes.
In some regions, tomato paste or red wine is added to enhance the taste.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from beef supports hemoglobin levels and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system health and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Carbohydrates from pasta
items.content: Pasta provides the energy needed for intense workouts and mental performance.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Beef can contain saturated fats, so choosing lean cuts is recommended.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared sauces or broths may add extra salt; control added sodium.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: If you have gluten intolerance, opt for gluten‑free pasta.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Beef should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C to avoid the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the beef stew with pasta hot, optionally topped with fresh herbs (parsley, basil) or grated Parmesan. The dish is convenient to pack in a container for lunch or a snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for 1‑2 months. Reheat thoroughly before consumption.
